title: Apple Watch Crash Detection calls 911 for Andi Burns, 19, trapped upside down in her pickup in the Little Miami River; Clermont County crews pull her out with bruises only
summary: On 22 Feb 2026 near Batavia, Ohio, a 19-year-old's truck flipped into the Little Miami River; Clermont County officials say her Apple Watch called 911 by Crash Detection and crews freed her.
account: Andi Burns, 19, was driving home from work on State Route 222 in Batavia Township, Clermont County, Ohio, on 22 February 2026 when, according to the Ohio State Highway Patrol accident report cited by ABC News, she lost control on black ice, hit a tree and went off an embankment into the Little Miami River; WLWT says the truck dropped down a 15-foot ravine and flipped. ABC News (4 March 2026) reports that 'According to Clermont County officials, Burns was wearing an Apple Watch that automatically called 911 using its crash detection feature', and body-camera footage released by the Clermont County Sheriff's Office shows a dispatcher keeping her on the line while Central Joint Fire-EMS District firefighters and sheriff's deputies smashed a window and pulled her out; first-year firefighter Tommy Jetter was first into the water. Burns had found a pocket of air of about four inches at the floorboard. The accident report says she walked away with bruises. Burns told WKRC (11 March 2026) that there was also 'a crash detection on the Live 360 that my mom had on her phone' and that it called the police and her family, so a second crash-detection service may have placed calls; WLWT and ABC attribute the 911 call to the Apple Watch.
purpose: Crash Detection is built to recognise a severe car crash from sensor data and call emergency services with the device's location if the wearer does not respond; this call was that purpose.
location: Batavia Township, Clermont County, Ohio, United States
taxonomy_note: None of the six types names a rescue; Accessibility is used because the device gave a trapped, submerged driver access to emergency services she could not otherwise reach, as in other wearable records. Protective response rather than harm prevented because the crash had already happened and the system's contribution was summoning help. The event rests on local and national news reports that cite the sheriff's body-camera video, the Ohio State Highway Patrol accident report and Clermont County officials; no official document was fetched directly.

ratings.reason: Rescuers and Burns describe a submerged cab with four to six inches of air; firefighter Jetter called her survival 'very, very, very lucky'. The call brought crews at night to a river crash; whether anyone else would have called is not documented, and the sources are news reports.

Clermont County dispatch received the automated call with a location and stayed on the line; the sheriff's office released the body-camera video. No agency statement on timing or resources was fetched.

ai_role.statement: ABC News, citing Clermont County officials, and WLWT say the Apple Watch's Crash Detection placed the 911 call; Apple's support page says the feature detects severe crashes from on-device sensor data and calls automatically after a countdown if the wearer does not respond. Burns also told WKRC that a Life360 crash-detection service on her mother's phone called police and family, so the watch may not have been the only alert. Only news reports were fetched; no dispatch log or agency statement was obtained.

produced_by: A supported Apple Watch (Series 8 or later, SE 2nd generation, Ultra) with Crash Detection on and a cellular or Wi-Fi path to emergency services
A severe crash (rollover into water) with the wearer unable to reach a phone
A dispatcher able to act on the automated call and location
must_hold: The on-device crash classifier recognises the impact as a severe car crash
The wearer does not dismiss the alert within the countdown
Responders can reach the transmitted location in time
